• Common name: Red root floater
  • Other names: Floating spurge, Apple Duckweed
  • Scientific name: Phyllantus fluitans
  • Minimum tank size: 5 gallons (about 20 litres)
  • Difficulty: Medium
  • Lighting: Moderate to high
  • Water hardness: Soft to moderately hard
  • Substrate: Not needed
  • Growth rate: Moderate to high
  • Placement in tank: Floating
  • Leaf size: 2–2.5 cm
  • Fertilizer: Recommended
  • CO2: Not needed
  • Propagation: From the stalks; it can also branch
Red root floater (Phyllantus fluitans) is indigenous to the Amazon River Basin in South America. The plant has also been spotted in some parts of North and Central America.
It grows as a free-floating aquatic plant on the surface of still or stagnant waters.
The recommended tank size for growing Red root floater is a minimum of 5 gallons (about 20 litres). It grows best in open, well-lit tanks.

Bèo rễ đỏ chỉ cần thả nổi lên mặt nước, không phải trồng xuống nền. Bèo mua về có thể mang theo ký sinh trùng, ốc hại, ấu trùng chuồn chuồn, hoặc đã bị xử lý bằng thuốc trừ sâu cực độc với cá, tép, ốc, nên cách ly trước rồi mới thả sang bể chính. Muốn giữ bèo ở một góc thì uốn một đoạn dây oxy thành vòng rồi thả bèo vào trong. Loài này không ưa nước động, mặt nước chỉ cần gợn nhẹ. Thấy bèo thối và chuyển nâu thì có thể do dòng chảy mạnh quá, giảm dòng xuống là được.

Red root floater is good for beginners since it is fairly easy to care for. Keep a few things in check and the plant will flourish all year round.

The plant is known for its deep red leaves and roots, so provide sufficient iron for the development of this reddish coloration. Use a good iron supplement and dose the aquarium water regularly, without overdoing it; always follow the manufacturer's instructions.

Prune excess foliage when it overcrowds the top layer of the tank and covers the whole surface. Otherwise the floating plants will completely shade the plants at the bottom, which is bad, especially if they are not low-light plants. Overcrowding also causes competition for resources and rapid depletion of nutrients, so prune on time and dispose of the cuttings properly.

Provide the essential macronutrients in the right doses, as the plants enjoy nutrient-rich water, and perform regular partial water changes to maintain excellent water quality, which curbs the growth of algae and diatoms.

High light makes the plants grow larger and bumpy, and they turn from green to pink-red or even deep red, and the roots attain their renowned bright red colour. Under low light, the plant has smaller, flatter, pale green leaves with only a small tinge of red.

Temperature: The optimal temperature is 22–26°C. The plant does not tolerate temperatures that are too low or too high, which can cause it to melt.

pH: Keep the pH between 6.5 and 7.5 for the best growth and health.

Hardness: The plant tolerates soft to moderately hard water, preferably in the range of 0–12 GH.

Lighting: Red root floater requires moderate to high lighting. An artificial light source such as an LED light serves this purpose best, as it does not emit heat into the aquarium water. More light is advisable in a hard water environment, whereas light intensity can be lower in soft water. Too much or too little light will harm the plants, so keep the light just bright enough and adjust it to the water conditions.

Substrate: Since the plant is a floating type, there is no specific substrate requirement.

Water flow: Provide gentle surface agitation. The plant appreciates gentle water flow similar to that in its natural habitat. Do not overdo it: in waters with high or turbulent flow, the plant will melt.

CO2 and fertilization: CO2 is not mandatory. As a floating plant, Red root floater has unlimited and constant access to carbon dioxide (CO2), which it uses for photosynthesis and growth. Fertilization, however, is needed because the plant takes a great deal of its nutrients from the tank water, so it is good to dose liquid fertilizers from time to time to replenish depleted nutrients and promote growth.

Important: If you keep shrimp in the tank with Red root floater, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilizers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Red root floater can be planted simply by floating the plantlets on the water surface. You can make a loop of airline tubing to confine the plants to a particular area instead of letting them drift around the top. Provide adequate nutrients and gentle water flow (they do not do well in waters with a lot of movement), and they will grow healthily and multiply rapidly.

Once established, the plant propagates by itself through side shoots. It can also be propagated easily by dividing the mature stalk between the clusters of roots and leaves, and by splitting already formed daughter plants.

Provide enough iron and bright lighting to boost the growth of the new plants; this rewards you with deep red coloration, healthy growth and more plants in the long run.

Origin and description

Red root floater belongs to the flowering plant family Phyllantaceae, with over 2000 species of trees, shrubs and herbs; it was formerly classified under the spurge family Euphorbiaceae. The largest genus in the family is Phyllantus, and the only aquatic species in it is Phyllantus fluitans.

Its name stems from its bright red roots. It has round, water-repellent, light green floating leaves that change colour with growing conditions. With ample lighting and a limited supply of nitrogen, the leaves can turn deep brown-red, reddish-purple or pink. The plant has thin submerged stems with abundant red roots and floating leaves with a heart-shaped base that conceals the stems. The leaves are typically about 2.5 cm and have a convex centre, while the leaf margins lie just level with the waterline. If conditions are favourable, the leaf axils bear tiny white flowers with six petals.

It looks similar to the floating fern Salvinia, but has just one floating leaf on each alternate node instead of the two found on Salvinia. Because of its deep red coloration, water-repellent leaves and slower growth compared with other floating plants, many aquarists choose it over Frogbit (bèo ếch), Dwarf Water lettuce (bèo cái lùn), Duckweed (bèo tấm) and similar plants.

Problems

Melting: This may result from too much flow, which makes the plants rot (turn brown), so provide a gentle flow. It can also be caused by excessive lighting; in that case reduce the intensity of the LED light and shorten the photoperiod significantly, and the plants will gradually return to normal health.

Overcrowding: Under the right conditions it grows fast and can cover the whole surface in a short time. This should be avoided because it blocks light from reaching other plants in the aquarium and stunts their growth.

Holes in leaves: Small holes in the leaves are often caused by potassium deficiency. Use potassium-rich fertilizers such as Flourish Advance to make up for the limited potassium in the aquarium water, and the plants should recover within a short time.

Benefits

  • Aesthetics: A nice-looking floating plant whose dense green foliage makes the aquarium look more natural.
  • Breeding ground: Provides a breeding ground for egg scatterers and dwarf shrimp.
  • Shelter / cover: Provides cover and shade for species that prefer low light; its submerged root-like leaves provide hiding spots for fry and juvenile fish.
  • Light penetration: It can also be used to filter light for plants that do not need much of it (for example Java Fern, Amazon Sword, Marimo Moss Ball, Anubias), diffusing very bright aquarium lighting.
  • Oxygenation: It oxygenates the tank water through photosynthesis and absorbs toxins harmful to aquatic life.
  • Algae control: It is extremely effective against algae, outcompeting algae for nutrients and suppressing its growth.
  • Removal of excess nutrients: It absorbs harmful compounds from fish waste, decayed plant matter and tap water, removing toxins such as ammonia, nitrates, nitrites and heavy metals. Because it grows rapidly, it needs lots of nutrients.

Tankmates

Red root floater is ideal for Betta tanks, as Bettas often roam the surface looking for food particles around the red roots. It can be planted in tanks with:

  • Fish (for example Bettas, Tetras, Zebra Danio, Platies, Guppies, Endlers, Mollies, Otocinclus Catfish, Pygmy Cory Catfish).
  • Snails (for example Japanese trapdoor snails, Ramshorn snails, Nerite snails, Malaysian Trumpet snails, Black Devil Snails, Asolene spixi, Rabbit Snails).
  • Dwarf shrimp (all varieties of Neocaridina such as Red Cherry, Blue Velvet, Black Rose, Snowball, Orange Sakura, Green Jade and Rili shrimp, or Caridina species such as Crystal Red, Caridina cf. babaulti and Blue Tiger shrimp, as well as Amano, Ghost, Bamboo and Vampire shrimp). Basically any shrimp species can be kept with it.
  • Crayfish and crabs. These animals are hard to keep in planted tanks, as most will try to uproot and eat everything. Floating plants are a good choice for them because they simply cannot reach them.

Avoid species that may find Red root floater palatable, e.g. Koi, Goldfish, Oscars, Rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, Clown loaches and African cichlids. These species can cause real problems in planted tanks.

Quarantine

Quarantine Red root floater before putting it into your aquarium.

  • The plant can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.).
  • It may also have been treated with chemicals (pesticides) to remove parasites, snails, etc. These chemicals are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Conclusion

Red root floater is a good addition to most kinds of tank set-ups and a great way to add a pop of red to your aquarium. This floating plant is inexpensive, attractive and a good substitute for plants like Duckweed that need more attention to stay in good condition.
